reason: The text depicts Abimelech, the central figure of authority, responding to criticism and challenges with military aggression and violence rather than humility. When Gaal questions his legitimacy (verse 28-29), Abimelech responds by setting an ambush and engaging in armed conflict (verses 34-41), not by humbly accepting or engaging with the criticism. Similarly, Jotham's fable (verses 7-20) serves as implicit moral criticism of Abimelech's rise to power and methods, yet there is no indication Abimelech responds with humility or self-reflection. The narrative concludes by explicitly stating that God returned Abimelech's evil upon his own head (verse 56), suggesting that his model of leadership—characterized by manipulation, violence, and aggressive responses to opposition—is morally condemned rather than upheld as exemplary. The text implicitly demonstrates that such leadership lacks humility and results in divine judgment.
